studyData.intro: A single red word gives this spare wrapper its centre of gravity. Compare the small black lines above and below, and keep the first-edition wrapper distinct from the later binding and internal title page included in the same library scan.

regions.label: Small author line
regions.summary: The author begins at a quiet scale.

sections.heading: Mário de Andrade
sections.body: The author’s name appears in small black capitals near the top. The spacing and modest scale create a narrow line rather than a large block, leaving the red title much stronger farther down the wrapper.

sections.heading: The first edition in São Paulo
sections.body: USP Brasiliana identifies this as the 1928 first edition of Mário de Andrade’s work, published in São Paulo. Its e.2 notation identifies the library’s second copy, not a second edition of the book.

regions.question: What changes if you imagine the author’s name enlarged to match the title?

regions.label: Rule under the author
regions.summary: A small line gives the opening a base.

sections.heading: A short dark support
sections.body: A narrow horizontal rule sits with the author line. It gives that small area a clear lower edge, separating the opening credit from the long interval of paper leading toward the red title.

sections.heading: A measured opening
sections.body: The rule can make the author credit feel deliberately placed rather than simply floating. Its thinness matters: a heavier bar would compete with the title, while this one quietly establishes a horizontal reference.

regions.question: Does the rule make the author line feel more formal or more separated from the rest?

regions.label: Red Macunaíma
regions.summary: The only large red word establishes the centre.

sections.heading: A name with an accent
sections.body: The title reads Macunaíma, including the accent on í. Its capital M and lower-case continuation form a recognisable word shape; the accent is part of the written name, not a decorative fleck to remove.

sections.heading: Colour and size reinforce one another
sections.body: The title is both substantially larger and warmer in colour than the other wording. Because those two signals agree, it dominates without needing an enclosing panel or an accompanying illustration.

regions.question: Which contributes more to the title’s prominence: its red colour or its scale?

regions.label: The accent over í
regions.kicker: A DETAIL ABOVE THE LETTER LINE
regions.summary: A small mark belongs to the word.

sections.heading: A detail above the letter line
sections.body: The accented vowel introduces a small mark above the main lower-case forms. It breaks the title’s upper contour and rewards closer viewing, while remaining part of the continuous red word rather than a separate emblem.

sections.heading: Accuracy in a familiar shape
sections.body: A title can seem recognisable even when one small mark is missing, but that does not make the omission neutral. Preserving the accent respects the actual printed wording and keeps visual simplification from silently rewriting the name.

regions.question: What other tiny marks would be easy to mistake for wear when reading an old printed cover?

regions.label: Small subtitle
regions.summary: A second phrase sits close beneath the title.

sections.heading: A compact description
sections.body: The displayed subtitle uses the historical spelling O heroi sem nenhum caracter, conventionally rendered “the hero without any character.” The phrase introduces a verbal ambiguity; it should not be reduced to a psychological judgement about a pictured person, since there is no portrait here.

sections.heading: Close enough to remain a unit
sections.body: The subtitle’s small black letters sit directly under the much larger red title. Their proximity joins the two lines, while their different scale and colour maintain a clear hierarchy within that compact middle group.

regions.question: How much space could you add before the subtitle began to feel unrelated to the title?

regions.label: Large quiet interval
regions.summary: Paper keeps the bottom imprint distant.

sections.heading: An extended unprinted area
sections.body: A large area of tan paper separates the subtitle from the bottom place and date. Surface spotting remains visible through that interval, but no major printed illustration or secondary title fills it.

sections.heading: Pacing with absence
sections.body: The gap lets the central name remain dominant and delays the small imprint. The viewer can move quickly from author to title, then slow down before the final publication information; that pacing is created by distance alone.

regions.question: Would an illustration in this interval strengthen the title or compete with it?

regions.label: São Paulo and 1928
regions.summary: Place and date close the wrapper.

sections.heading: A small historical line
sections.body: The lower imprint gives São Paulo and 1928, beneath a short rule. Its size makes it secondary to the title, but it provides information that cannot be inferred from the colour or typography alone.

sections.heading: A wrapper for a specific edition
sections.body: The library record supports the first-edition date and São Paulo publication context. These small printed details help distinguish this wrapper from a later reprint or from the separate internal title page in the same digitized volume.

regions.question: Why is a small imprint useful when several different covers circulate for the same literary work?

regions.label: Paper and scan edges
regions.summary: The reproduction retains its physical history.

sections.heading: Spots across quiet areas
sections.body: Brown spotting and uneven tan colour are especially visible where the design leaves paper exposed. A dark photographed surround and the wrapper’s slightly irregular edge remain visible, distinguishing the sheet from a newly typeset facsimile.

sections.heading: The correct page in the scan
sections.body: The displayed image is the wrapper on PDF page 7 of USP item bbm/8935. The scan also includes an outer binding and an internal title page; substituting either would change the object being analysed.

regions.question: How would a clean modern recreation conceal differences between design, paper and later wear?
